main.title: Radiata Stories
main.subtitle: A city whose inhabitants have places to be
main.summary: Radiata Stories is tri-Ace's PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in Japan on 27 January 2005. Jack Russell enters a world of knights, guilds and neighbouring peoples, but much of its character comes from the individuals living around him. Town residents follow daily routines, going to work and returning home instead of waiting permanently in one place. The player learns the city by noticing those movements. Meeting someone can depend on when and where they are approached, making ordinary observation part of building a party and discovering the world.

cards.heading: A city whose inhabitants have places to be
cards.text: Radiata Stories is tri-Ace's PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in Japan on 27 January 2005. Jack Russell enters a world of knights, guilds and neighbouring peoples, but much of its character comes from the individuals living around him. Town residents follow daily routines, going to work and returning home instead of waiting permanently in one place. The player learns the city by noticing those movements. Meeting someone can depend on when and where they are approached, making ordinary observation part of building a party and discovering the world.

cards.heading: Learn a routine, then make a connection
cards.text: Characters have their own jobs, homes, personalities and schedules. The day-and-night system gives those details practical consequences, as a person encountered in one place may be elsewhere later. Exploring therefore means paying attention to the habits of the population as well as the geography of the streets. Recruitment grows from those meetings and the tasks attached to them, connecting the party to the larger community. The city gradually becomes more familiar because the player understands who uses it, not only because every doorway has been opened once.

cards.heading: An adventure remembered for its population
cards.text: Naoki Akiyama directed the game, with Noriyuki Iwadare composing the soundtrack. Its action combat sits alongside a world whose people provide many reasons to return to familiar places. The North American release followed in September 2005. Reception was mixed at launch, but the game developed a lasting following for its character and approach to everyday life. Radiata Stories makes a useful distinction within the role-playing genre: a large cast can be more than a list of recruits when each member appears to have a life continuing outside the player's immediate journey.

main.title: Shadow of Rome
main.subtitle: Two routes through a Roman conspiracy
main.summary: Shadow of Rome is Capcom's PlayStation 2 action-adventure, first released in Europe on 4 February 2005. A fictional account of Julius Caesar's assassination follows Agrippa, whose father is accused of the murder, and Octavianus, who investigates the charge. Their activities divide the game between gladiatorial combat and stealth. One character must survive in front of a crowd while the other searches for information without drawing attention. The contrast gives the same conspiracy two practical forms: a public struggle for survival and a quieter effort to uncover what happened.

cards.heading: Two routes through a Roman conspiracy
cards.text: Shadow of Rome is Capcom's PlayStation 2 action-adventure, first released in Europe on 4 February 2005. A fictional account of Julius Caesar's assassination follows Agrippa, whose father is accused of the murder, and Octavianus, who investigates the charge. Their activities divide the game between gladiatorial combat and stealth. One character must survive in front of a crowd while the other searches for information without drawing attention. The contrast gives the same conspiracy two practical forms: a public struggle for survival and a quieter effort to uncover what happened.

cards.heading: Win the attention of the arena
cards.text: Agrippa's sections place weapons, enemies and the audience within a single violent performance. The player has to survive the immediate fight while making use of the equipment and opportunities around the arena. Combat becomes an exaggerated spectacle, with the crowd responding to what happens in front of it. Octavianus changes the pace through infiltration and investigation, where avoiding discovery takes priority over direct force. Alternating between the two characters gives the campaign its structure, making progress in the larger mystery depend on very different kinds of action.

cards.heading: A planned series takes another direction
cards.text: Motohide Eshiro directed the game, with Keiji Inafune and Yoshinori Ono producing and Yoshino Aoki and Kota Suzuki composing its music. Reviews generally welcomed the gladiatorial combat and presentation, while the slower stealth sections attracted more criticism. Capcom had begun work towards a sequel, but disappointing sales changed the plan. That follow-up developed into Dead Rising instead. Shadow of Rome therefore stands as an unusual single release, joining historical conspiracy to theatrical violence at a moment when Capcom was exploring new projects for a wider international audience.

main.title: Champions: Return to Arms
main.subtitle: Decide what to do with a defeated god
main.summary: Champions: Return to Arms is Snowblind Studios' PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in North America on 7 February 2005. After the defeat of Innoruuk, fragments of his essence are scattered across the Planes of Power. The player can work to destroy those shards or collect them for his return, giving the campaign two opposing purposes. The familiar combination of exploration, combat and equipment remains the centre of play. A choice about the world's future supplies another reason to lead a party through its dangerous places.

cards.heading: Decide what to do with a defeated god
cards.text: Champions: Return to Arms is Snowblind Studios' PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in North America on 7 February 2005. After the defeat of Innoruuk, fragments of his essence are scattered across the Planes of Power. The player can work to destroy those shards or collect them for his return, giving the campaign two opposing purposes. The familiar combination of exploration, combat and equipment remains the centre of play. A choice about the world's future supplies another reason to lead a party through its dangerous places.

cards.heading: Build a character while clearing the route
cards.text: Character classes provide different starting capabilities, from direct fighters to spellcasters and healers. Battles and quests award experience, allowing the player to strengthen a chosen role as the journey continues. New equipment gives a more immediate way to change how an encounter is handled. Cooperative play adds the question of how several characters can help one another instead of pursuing the same task independently. The campaign's opposing paths visit the same broad locations with different objectives, so the purpose of a journey can change even when parts of the route remain familiar.

cards.heading: Return to Norrath with company
cards.text: Up to four players can share the adventure, with online support originally allowing a group to form beyond the living room. Inon Zur returned to compose the score, maintaining a musical connection to Champions of Norrath. Ubisoft published the European edition in March 2005. The sequel develops the earlier game's direct approach to the EverQuest setting, using a manageable cooperative adventure rather than the structure of a persistent online world. Its continuing attraction is the group itself: the equipment collected and abilities learned become tools for facing the next area together.

main.title: Star Fox: Assault
main.subtitle: From Rail Shooter to Battlefield
main.summary: Star Fox: Assault returns Fox McCloud to combat on GameCube, with Namco developing and Nintendo publishing.

cards.heading: Fox leaves the cockpit
cards.text: Star Fox: Assault returns Fox McCloud to combat on GameCube, with Namco developing and Nintendo publishing. Its 2005 adventure moves between aerial battles, ground vehicles and action on foot. The familiar Arwing is one part of the battlefield rather than Fox's only place within it.

cards.heading: Three ways across a battlefield
cards.text: An Arwing offers speed and flight; a Landmaster tank brings heavy ground fire; Fox can also run and use handheld weapons. Those changes alter the scale of a location. Something crossed quickly from the air can become cover, a target or a route when approached on the ground.

cards.heading: Four views of the same fight
cards.text: The local multiplayer mode supports four people in split screen. Vehicles and on-foot combat become tools in a shared space, with each player watching a different view of the action. It preserves a familiar living-room arrangement: one console, several controllers and everyone close enough to see a rival's reaction.

main.title: Devil May Cry 3: Dante's Awakening
main.subtitle: Four Styles to Reinvent Dante
main.summary: Devil May Cry 3 looks back to an earlier Dante and his conflict with his twin brother Vergil.

cards.heading: Before the familiar Dante
cards.text: Devil May Cry 3 looks back to an earlier Dante and his conflict with his twin brother Vergil. Its 2005 PlayStation 2 release makes that rivalry the centre of an action game built around a growing collection of melee weapons, firearms and fighting styles.

cards.heading: Choose a style
cards.text: The original game asks the player to choose a style before a mission or at a Divinity Statue. Trickster, Swordmaster, Gunslinger and Royal Guard offer different priorities, with further styles unlocked later. That choice shapes the tools available during a difficult encounter rather than merely changing Dante's appearance.

cards.heading: Free Style arrives in the Switch edition
cards.text: Capcom's 2020 Switch edition added Free Style mode, allowing styles to change during a fight. The original 2005 release required a choice before a mission or at a Divinity Statue. This later option expands the combinations a player can perform, showing how a reissue can revise combat as well as bring it to another platform.

main.title: FIFA Street
main.summary: FIFA Street is a sports video game developed by EA Canada and published by Electronic Arts under the EA Sports BIG label.

cards.heading: Football moves into the street
cards.text: FIFA Street is a sports video game developed by EA Canada and published by Electronic Arts under the EA Sports BIG label. It is commentated on by MC Harvey of the So Solid Crew. It was released in February 2005 for PlayStation 2, Xbox, and GameCube. The cover features Brazilian international footballer Ronaldinho.

cards.heading: Building a match around tricks
cards.text: FIFA Street adapts football to the arcade approach of EA's NFL Street and NBA Street. Smaller teams compete through flair, tricks and style, drawing on freestyle football played in streets and backlots. The emphasis gives a match a different character from the team formations and tactics of EA's conventional FIFA Football series.

cards.heading: Earning respect and recruiting stars
cards.text: Using reputation and respect gained from playing 4-on-4 games with tricks and flair, the aim of FIFA Street is to build a team up of well-known and recognised players including Ronaldo and Ronaldinho to progress through street venues across the world.

cards.heading: Success on PlayStation 2
cards.text: The PlayStation 2 version of FIFA Street received a "Platinum" sales award from the Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association (ELSPA), indicating sales of at least 300,000 copies in the United Kingdom.

main.title: Another Code: Two Memories
main.subtitle: A letter from a missing father
main.summary: Another Code: Two Memories is Cing's Nintendo DS mystery adventure about thirteen-year-old Ashley Mizuki Robbins. A letter leads her to Blood Edward Island in search of the father she believed was dead. The player moves Ashley through three-dimensional locations while examining closer views, objects and photographs. Known as Trace Memory in North America, the game places a quiet investigation inside the unfamiliar shape of Nintendo's new handheld. Looking carefully and trying the machine's different inputs become part of discovering what happened to her family.

cards.heading: A letter from a missing father
cards.text: Another Code: Two Memories is Cing's Nintendo DS mystery adventure about thirteen-year-old Ashley Mizuki Robbins. A letter leads her to Blood Edward Island in search of the father she believed was dead. The player moves Ashley through three-dimensional locations while examining closer views, objects and photographs. Known as Trace Memory in North America, the game places a quiet investigation inside the unfamiliar shape of Nintendo's new handheld. Looking carefully and trying the machine's different inputs become part of discovering what happened to her family.

cards.heading: Evidence on two screens
cards.text: The lower screen provides an overhead view for moving Ashley, using either the stylus or the directional pad. The upper screen supplies a closer image of the current location. Selecting something worth examining brings it into the investigation, where an ordinary object may conceal the next clue. Ashley also carries an electronic device called the DAS, named DTS in North America. It reads data cards and stores photographs. Information is therefore something the player can collect, revisit and compare rather than simply hear once in a conversation.

cards.heading: A machine made for a mystery
cards.text: Puzzles draw on the touchscreen and microphone, asking the player to consider the DS itself as a set of tools. Ashley's camera can retain a limited collection of pictures, making a photograph useful as evidence as well as a record of a place. These actions suit the story's concern with uncertain memories: an answer may depend on examining something again with another piece of information. Cing makes the small, personal act of handling a portable machine feel appropriate to a young character investigating her own history.
